title: 6  Fall 2026 Roadmap — experiments to December
text:
6.1 Research questions
Working plan from today (Aug 20) to the results in December/January. The top-level Gantt is the source of truth for dates; this page holds the reasoning behind them: research questions, week-level milestones, the quantifiables spec (metrics, generalization tiers, failure taxonomy), the literature map, the open-source stack, and how AI research assistants are used. Revise it whenever the plan changes, it becomes the skeleton of the Methods chapter and the defense timeline slide.
The thesis claim is built around three questions. Every experiment should answer one of them.
RQ1 — Adaptation. Can current open vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models (NVIDIA GR00T N1.5, SmolVLA, optionally π0) be adapted to a new embodiment, the OARbot (Clearpath Dingo omni base + Kinova Jaco Gen2 6-DOF arm) with a modest demonstration dataset collected in the lab?
RQ2 — Comparison & generalization. On a fixed task suite, how do the fine-tuned VLAs compare against each other and against a from-scratch imitation baseline (ACT) trained only on our demonstrations, both on in-distribution success rate and on how performance degrades across generalization tiers (unseen poses, distractors, novel object instances, paraphrased instructions)? The baseline is what makes generalization attributable: if the VLAs degrade less than ACT out of distribution, that gap is the measured value of internet-scale pretraining.
RQ3 — Practicality. What are the real compute and data costs, fine-tuning wall-clock on a DGX Spark, demos-per-task needed, on-robot inference rates, and what does that imply for small-lab replication?
RQ3 is the differentiator: most VLA papers report results on the authors’ hardware fleet; a careful research of what it takes to adapt these models on one robot with two lab machines is a new contribution.

title: 6  Fall 2026 Roadmap — experiments to December
text:
6.3 Month-by-month plan

6.3.1 September — bring-up, task suite, literature (epics B1, A2, A1)

Week of Sep 1: Full teleop chain on one OARbot: drive the base, command the arm (SpaceMouse), stream both Azure Kinects. Verify E-stop. Note which sensors are actually usable (docs already flag the UWB units as inoperable).
Week of Sep 8: Record demonstrations into LeRobotDataset format: joint states + (base velocity, future proof) + camera frames, replay a recorded episode open-loop on the robot to prove the pipeline is lossless. This replay test is very important to corroborate the strategy works.
Week of Sep 15: Freeze the task suite (epic A2): 3 tasks in increasing difficulty, e.g. (T1) tabletop pick-and-place, arm only; (T2) fetch and navigate to a table, grasp, return; (T3) a true mobile-manipulation task with base+arm coordination (open a door, clear a table). Define per-task success criteria, the staged progress rubric (reach / grasp / transport / place), the in-distribution randomization grid, and the generalization tiers G1–G4 (see the quantifiables spec below) before collecting data. Confirm the suite with the advisor. Also start the action-space decision log: every embodiment-design choice (joint deltas vs. absolutes, base twist representation, chunk length, control rates, normalization) gets a dated entry with the reasoning, this log becomes the Methods section on adapting VLA action heads to a mobile manipulator.
Week of Sep 22: Pilot data collection: ~10 episodes per task, train a quick SmolVLA sanity run on T1, fix whatever breaks.
Gate 1 (Sep 26): teleop + record + replay all work, task suite signed off. Fallback if late: drop T3 base motion and run an arm-centric thesis, decide here.


6.3.1.1 Data-pipeline decisions (locked 2026-08-25)

Teleop is Cartesian (SpaceMouse → EE twist → Kinova IK); training actions are joint positions derived from achieved states: action(t) = joint angles at t+Δ. Teleop space and training space are decoupled by this labeling — the raw SpaceMouse commands are never used as labels.
Recording = ros2 bag record on the helper laptop (compressed image topics, one auto-numbered bag per episode), then an offline bag → LeRobotDataset converter: uniform rate, nearest-frame alignment, the frozen 10-D schema, t+Δ action labels, instruction string per episode. Raw bags are kept forever as source of truth — every labeling choice stays reversible without re-collection.
Wrist camera mounted before any kept demos — observations are locked in at recording time; actions can be re-derived, images cannot.



6.3.1.2 Week-1 verification checklist (at the robot)

ros2 topic list + ros2 topic hz during teleop: arm JointState topic (finger joints included?), camera topics, /odom, raw teleop command topic if exposed. Note exact names and rates.
Angular control — does the lab stack expose joint position/velocity streaming to the Gen2? Teleop only proves the Cartesian path; policies need the joint path. Biggest unknown on the platform. (Resolved 2026-08-26: the kinova-ros2 driver streams in/joint_velocity at exactly 100 Hz — see the platform notes.)
Gripper commands land on a ROS topic and appear in recordings.
Round-trip latency: camera → RTX box → command back to the helper laptop (decides wireless inference viability; chunk ≈ 3× latency).
Clock sync (chrony) across Dingo PC / helper laptop / NUC / RTX box — required for correct chunk alignment at deployment.
End-to-end proof: record one episode → convert → replay it on the arm via angular control.




6.3.2 October — dataset at scale + first baseline (epics B2, C2)

Weeks of Oct 5 / Oct 12: Main collection push, target 50–100 episodes per task (ACT/SmolVLA-class results are routinely reported around 50 demos/task; more helps T3). Interleave tasks and vary object poses per the randomization grid. Nightly QC script: episode counts, joint-limit outliers, dropped frames.
Week of Oct 19: SmolVLA fine-tuned per-task on the Spark, and ACT trained from scratch on the identical data — it trains in hours and rides along on the same LeRobot dataset, giving the no-pretraining reference point for RQ2. First closed-loop rollouts on the robot.
Week of Oct 26: Start GR00T N1.5 fine-tuning (epic C1) — the new-embodiment head needs the most debugging lead time. First structured mini-eval (10 trials/task) of SmolVLA.
Gate 2 (Oct 31): SmolVLA achieves non-zero success on T1 with a documented eval protocol. If zero: freeze collection, debug the data/normalization/camera pipeline first — more bad data won’t help.



6.3.3 November — GR00T + full evaluation (epics C1, C3)

Weeks of Nov 2 / Nov 9: GR00T N1.5 tuned across tasks; top-up data collection where QC shows gaps; π0 (LoRA via LeRobot/openpi) only if both main models are stable.
Week of Nov 16: Full evaluation begins (epic C3): ≥20 trials/task/policy on the shared in-distribution grid, everything in the quantifiables spec logged per trial, video of every trial. Budget realistically — 3 tasks × 4 policies (ACT, SmolVLA, GR00T, π0-if-attempted) × 20 trials at ~3 min/trial is ~12 robot-hours per full round, plus resets.
Gate 3 (Nov 27): Decide final comparison set (ACT + 2 or 3 VLAs) and confirm the data-scale ablation (retrain at 25/50/100 demos on one task) fits the calendar.



6.3.4 December — finish, freeze, outline (epics C3, D)

Weeks of Dec 1 / Dec 7: Complete in-distribution eval rounds + data-scale ablation; generalization round — tiers G1–G4 on each model’s best checkpoint only (10 trials/tier, see quantifiables spec).
Week of Dec 14: Re-runs and holes only. Results freeze Dec 18 — after this date, no new experiments, only analysis.
Week of Dec 21: All results tables and figures generated by script from logged data; chapter outline drafted in chapters/.



6.3.5 January–March 2027
Chapter drafts Jan 4 – Feb 26 (Background and Methods first — most of Methods should fall out of this page and the epic READMEs), full draft to advisor end of February, defense mid-March (confirm the exact date and committee logistics with the advisor in September, not January).

section: 6.4 Quantifiables — what gets measured and reported
text:
6.4 Quantifiables — what gets measured and reported
What the results chapter must contain, modeled on what this class of papers (ACT, Diffusion Policy, OpenVLA, π0, SmolVLA, GR00T, Mobile ALOHA) actually reports. Frozen in epic A2 before data collection; every eval trial logs a row with all of these fields plus a video path.

6.4.1 Decision thresholds — what “achieved” means
Targets are pre-registered thresholds, not promises. A miss, analyzed honestly, is still a result.

Platform validated: ≥1 policy reaches ≥70% success on T1 in-distribution.
Pretraining transfer confirmed: the VLAs beat from-scratch ACT on the generalization tiers by ≥15 percentage points average. A null or negative gap = “pretraining did not pay off at this data scale on this embodiment”, a publishable negative result.
Practicality documented: complete cost sheet (below) for every model, no gaps.



6.4.2 Primary metrics (every policy, every task)








Metric
Definition
Reported as




Success rate
Binary per trial against the frozen rubric; human intervention = failure
% with 95% Wilson CI, n ≥ 20


Progress score
Staged credit: reach 0.25 / grasp 0.5 / transport 0.75 / place 1.0 (per-task rubric)
Mean 0–1; separates “never grasps” from “drops at the end” when success rates are low


Time to completion
Successful trials only, start signal → success condition
Median [IQR] seconds





6.4.3 Secondary metrics








Metric
Definition
Reported as




Inference latency
Camera frame in → action chunk out, on the RTX workstation
ms per chunk + achieved control rate (Hz)


Generalization gap
In-distribution success minus per-tier success
Percentage points, per tier per policy


Data efficiency
Success rate at 25 / 50 / 100 training demos (one task, all policies)
Curve — the small-lab money figure





6.4.4 Generalization tiers (RQ2)
Evaluated on each model’s best checkpoint only, 10 trials/tier, selection rules frozen in A2:

G0 — in-distribution: objects and poses from the training grid.
G1 — spatial: object poses outside the training grid.
G2 — visual: distractor objects + lighting change.
G3 — object: novel instance of the same category (different mug, different box).
G4 — language: paraphrased instruction, same task (“pick up the cup” → “grab the mug”). VLA-only tier — ACT has no language input, which is itself part of the comparison story.



6.4.5 Failure taxonomy
Every failed trial gets a first-failure label from this closed list, logged at eval time (10 seconds of effort) with the video path:
perception/grounding (approached wrong object) · navigation/base-pose (stopped out of reach) · grasp (contact but slip/miss) · manipulation-trajectory (jerky/unsafe motion, joint limit) · instruction (did the wrong task) · stall/timeout · hardware (excluded and retried, not counted).
Rendered as stacked bars per policy × task — this figure explains why the success rates differ and is the backbone of the analysis chapter.


6.4.6 Practicality cost sheet (RQ3)
Per model: fine-tuning wall-clock hours and peak memory on the DGX Spark, trainable parameter count (LoRA vs. full), GPU-hours per training run, on-robot inference hardware requirements. Plus data cost: minutes per collected episode, total collection hours, retake rate.


6.4.7 Deliverables checklist (results chapter)

T1 Main results: success ± CI, task × policy, in-distribution
T2 Generalization matrix: policy × tier
T3 Efficiency: latency, control rate, completion time
T4 Cost sheet (RQ3)
F1 Data-scale curve · F2 Failure-mode stacked bars · F3 Qualitative rollout film-strips (best + worst per policy)

Protocol hygiene: the randomization grid and rubrics are frozen before collection; checkpoint selection criteria defined before eval; all runs reported (no cherry-picked seeds); every trial has video.

title: 6  Fall 2026 Roadmap — experiments to December
text:
6.5 Literature map
Organized by the Background chapter’s likely sections. Maintain citations in Zotero and export to references.bib (keep BibTeX keys stable). Verify every reference on arXiv/Semantic Scholar before it enters the bib file — never cite from an LLM’s memory.
1. Learning from demonstration — foundations

Argall, Chernova, Veloso, Browning (2009), A survey of robot learning from demonstration — the canonical survey to anchor the chapter.
Pomerleau (1988), ALVINN — behavioral cloning origin.
Ross, Gordon, Bagnell (2011), DAgger — compounding-error argument every IL thesis needs.

2. Modern imitation learning architectures

Zhao et al. (RSS 2023), ACT / ALOHA — action chunking; the direct ancestor of today’s VLA action heads.
Chi et al. (RSS 2023), Diffusion Policy — generative action heads.
Lipman et al. (ICLR 2023), Flow Matching — theory behind π0-style and GR00T-style flow action heads.
Fu, Zhao, Finn (2024), Mobile ALOHA — the closest published setup to this thesis: whole-body IL on a mobile manipulator.

3. Vision-language-action models

Brohan et al., RT-1 (2022) and RT-2 (2023) — the VLA lineage.
Open X-Embodiment collaboration (2023/24) — cross-embodiment pretraining; why adapting a generalist to OARbot is plausible at all.
Octo Model Team (2024) — open generalist policy.
Kim et al. (2024), OpenVLA — open 7B VLA + fine-tuning recipes (see also the OpenVLA-OFT follow-up on efficient fine-tuning).
Black et al. (2024), π0; Physical Intelligence (2025), π0.5 — flow matching VLA, open weights via openpi.
Hugging Face (2025), SmolVLA — small (~450M) VLA designed for exactly this compute class; likely the workhorse baseline.
NVIDIA (2025), GR00T N1 paper (+ N1.5 release notes) — the primary model; its dual-system architecture and new-embodiment fine-tuning story are directly load-bearing.
Google DeepMind (2025), Gemini Robotics — closed, but frames the state of the art in Background.

4. Mobile manipulation and assistive context

TidyBot (2023), HomeRobot/OVMM (2023), BEHAVIOR-1K (2023) — mobile-manipulation task framing and benchmarks.
RPI’s own OARbot publications — get the list from the advisor; the assistive-robotics motivation should cite the lab’s line of work.

5. Datasets and evaluation methodology

DROID (2024), BridgeData V2 (2023), AgiBot World (2025) — large-scale teleop dataset practice worth imitating at small scale.
LIBERO (2023) — task-suite design and eval discipline.
SimplerEnv — Li et al. (2024), Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation — the real-vs-sim eval gap.
Recent work on statistically sound robot policy evaluation (trial counts, confidence intervals, A/B protocols) — good target for a deep-research sweep, see below.

6.7 Using AI research assistants
Division of labor — each tool where it is strongest:

Gemini Deep Research breadth: one report per Background section above (“annotated bibliography of VLA fine-tuning on novel embodiments 2023–2026, with arXiv links”). Also the eval-methodology sweep in §5.

Standing rule: LLM output is a lead, never a citation. Every claim that survives into the thesis gets verified against the primary source, and every reference is checked on arXiv before entering references.bib.

Compressed findings from digesting the OARbot documentation (oarbots repo · docs site · kinova-ros2) before first contact with the robot, plus the reconnaissance checklist for the first lab session. Feeds epic B1; the reasoning behind the pipeline lives in the Fall 2026 roadmap. Update this page as the topic dump and rate measurements replace assumptions with numbers.

title: 7  OARbot platform notes — findings & day-1 checklist
text:
7.1.1 Network and middleware

ROS 2 Jazzy with CycloneDDS (RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_cyclonedds_cpp) on the lab Wi-Fi CII8218-oarbots. Not Fast DDS — keep this machine’s env separate from the Isaac Sim / SO-101 setup.
Discovery is peer-to-peer (no master): any machine on the Wi-Fi with domain ID 0 sees everything. Connectivity check: ros2 topic list.
Domain layout: each robot runs internally in its own ROS domain — Blue = 2, Silver = 1 — and a domain bridge re-publishes both onto the shared domain 0 with /oarbot_blue/… and /oarbot_silver/… prefixes. The bridge is bidirectional: sensor streams out, commands in.
Multi-network trouble → pin the interface in ~/.ros/cyclonedds.xml and set CYCLONEDDS_URI.



7.1.2 Hardware (per robot)







Component
Detail




Base
Clearpath Dingo DO-100, mecanum (omnidirectional), onboard PC runs its ROS nodes


Arm
Kinova Jaco Gen2 6-DOF, 3-finger (j2n6s300), USB to helper laptop


Helper laptop
Lenovo ThinkPad on the base; runs kinova_driver + Kinect node, auto-launches at boot


Cameras
Azure Kinect on each arm (RGB-D, 30 fps max); overhead Kinect on a NUC does ArUco pose estimation (Blue tag 0, Silver tag 4)


F/T sensor
Bota Rokubi Gen0 at the wrist — enables admittance (kinesthetic) mode


Teleop
Surface Go 2 tablet: SpaceMouse Compact + deadman switch + E-stop; GUI via tablet_launch.sh


Inoperable
UWB units (DecaWave MDEK1001) — ignore



Boot order is strict (nodes fail to launch otherwise): batteries → Dingo → arm (hold home) → helper laptop → NUC (replug Kinect USB) → tablet → disengage E-stop → launch GUI.


7.1.3 The arm interface (kinova-ros2)
Topic names below are the stock driver names; on the lab network they appear under the bridge prefix (exact names TBC from the topic dump).









Direction
Topic
Type / unit
Notes




out
…driver/out/joint_state
sensor_msgs/JointState, rad
primary proprioception


out
…driver/out/tool_pose
end-effector pose



out
…driver/out/tool_wrench
wrist wrench



out
…driver/out/finger_position
finger state



in
…driver/in/joint_velocity
kinova_msgs/JointVelocity, deg/s
must publish at exactly 100 Hz


in
…driver/in/cartesian_velocity
kinova_msgs/PoseVelocity
same 100 Hz requirement



Services: home_arm, start/stop, start_force_control/stop_force_control (the tablet’s admittance button), set_zero_torques. Actions: joint trajectory, pose goal, fingers (percent/mm/turns).
Three load-bearing facts from the driver README:

100 Hz is exact, not a minimum. The arm’s DSP loops every 10 ms; slower publishing fails to reach the commanded velocity, faster does nothing. Any policy or teleop source must run through a 100 Hz command repeater.
Publishing stops ⇒ motion stops. The velocity stream is a built-in deadman — killing the publisher halts the arm.
Unit trap: commands in deg/s, joint states in rad. Convert in exactly one place in the pipeline; log the choice in the action-space decision log.



7.1.4 Control-rate design (why the policy loop is ~10 Hz)
Two decoupled rates, connected by action chunking: the decision loop (model inference) at ~10 Hz, the command stream at 100 Hz fed by a repeater executing the current action chunk. The decision rate is bounded by the camera (30 fps ceiling), model latency (ACT ~ms, but SmolVLA/GR00T/π0 are 50–200 ms per chunk on the RTX workstation), and end-to-end Wi-Fi latency. Published VLAs run 1–10 Hz re-planning with high-rate chunk execution (π0: 50 Hz chunks, ~2 Hz model calls). Achieved latency/control rate is an RQ3 metric — measured per model, not assumed.


7.1.5 Pipeline decisions locked in so far

Bag-first recording: ros2 bag record (one bag per episode, keypress wrapper) is the recorder node — record generously (joints, RGB, depth, wrench, odom, both command topics, /tf, camera_info). Converter script resamples offline to a fixed policy-rate clock and emits LeRobotDataset; converter bugs cost a re-run, not a re-collection.
Action labels come from achieved states, not raw teleop (locked 2026-08-25): teleop stays Cartesian (SpaceMouse → EE twist → Kinova IK), while training actions are joint positions at t+Δ derived from the recorded joint states — teleop space and training space are decoupled. Details in the roadmap’s data-pipeline decisions.
Replay test is rung 0 of the model ladder: republish a recorded episode’s commands at original timing; the arm must reproduce the demo before any learning starts. Ladder: replay → ACT → SmolVLA → GR00T N1.5 → (π0).
Inference node mirrors the recorder: same topics in, same preprocessing as training (normalization stats ship with the checkpoint), chunk execution + 100 Hz repeater out, keyboard deadman publishing zeros, human at the E-stop. Dry-run the plumbing with a dummy policy (zeros / replayed chunk) before the first trained model.
Admittance mode is a candidate second demo modality (kinesthetic guiding via the F/T sensor) — bake off against SpaceMouse teleop in the pilot week; docs warn calibration can be flaky, keep E-stop close.

All exit criteria met. Plain-language account in the lab notebook; raw dumps and command captures in WSL ~/oarbot_recon_2026-08-27/.

Env sanity ✓ — plus the unplanned fixes that made discovery work from WSL at all: mirrored networking, lab Wi-Fi marked Private, and the decisive Hyper-V firewall rule (inbound UDP 7400–7500 into WSL); ~/.ros/cyclonedds-oarbot.xml (interface pin

unicast peers) wired into .bashrc.

Inventory dumps ✓ — 49 topics, 25 nodes, 176 services, 8 actions (only Blue was powered).
Rates ✓ — combined /oarbot_blue/joint_states (16 joints: 4 wheels + 6 arm + 6 fingers, standard JointState) at ~9.7 Hz; Kinect 1920×1080 at ~14.6 fps internally, raw RGB arriving at only ~3.4 Hz over Wi-Fi.
Camera transport ✓ — no /compressed topics exist; Wi-Fi drops ~75 % of raw frames → record on the helper laptop, as the Aug 25 data-pipeline decision anticipated.
Command topics ✓ — identified in tablet_gui source and confirmed by live capture (1,073 messages): arm = PoseVelocity on in/cartesian_velocity at ~119 Hz while the deadman is held; fingers = PoseVelocityWithFingers (closure %) event-based on in/cartesian_velocity_with_fingers; base = TwistStamped on dingo/cmd_vel. Quirk: Silver’s x-y axes are flipped in the tablet source. Reading these types required building kinova_msgs locally (deactivate conda first — CMake prefers the CONDA_PREFIX Python).
Clock check ✓ — laptop ≈ 1 s ahead of robot stamps. Harmless for recording (helper laptop = single clock for camera + joints); chrony required before live deployment.
Command authority ✓ — 150 PoseVelocity messages at 100 Hz (twist_linear_z: 0.02) sent from the laptop raised the arm ~3 cm; motion stopped when publishing stopped. External control confirmed — the exact channel a policy will use.

Next per the roadmap: the recording pipeline on the helper laptop (ros2 bag record, one bag per episode).

title: 8  Lab notebook
text:
8.1 2026-08-27 — Day 1 with the robot
Session-by-session record of hands-on work with the robots, newest first — one dated entry per session, written so both an advisor and a non-engineer can follow it. The technical reference behind these entries is the platform notes; formal weekly summaries live in the weekly updates.

title: 8  Lab notebook
text:
8.1.1 The goal
Before a robot can learn anything, my laptop and the robot have to talk to each other. Today’s job was to establish that conversation: hear everything the robot senses, and prove my laptop can tell the robot what to do — the two pipes that all the thesis work will flow through.


8.1.2 What happened
Getting connected took detective work. The robot speaks over the lab’s Wi-Fi, but my laptop runs its robot software inside a Linux compartment (WSL), and Windows was silently guarding that compartment’s door: security rules dropped the robot’s replies before they arrived. Everything looked configured correctly and nothing worked — until we found the right firewall gate to open. This is now fixed permanently; the laptop connects on its own from here on.
Then the robot came through loud and clear. We catalogued everything it broadcasts — 49 data channels — and watched its joint angles stream live in a terminal while I drove the arm with the teleoperation tablet.
We caught the tablet’s commands mid-flight. While I teleoperated, my laptop recorded over a thousand of the exact command messages the tablet sends the arm. This matters because a learned policy will speak through this same channel — now we know its precise format: six speed values (move/turn in each direction) plus one gripper number. Seven numbers, a hundred times a second. That is the language the robot is commanded in.
And the finale: my laptop moved the arm. A two-second command stream sent from my keyboard raised the arm three centimetres, smoothly, and it stopped by itself — with a hand on the emergency stop the whole time. External control: proven.


8.1.3 The numbers that shape what comes next








Measurement
Value
Consequence




Joint angle updates
~10 per second
matches the planned learning rate


Camera (on the robot)
15 images/sec, full HD
healthy at the source


Camera (over Wi-Fi)
only ~3.4 images/sec arrive
Wi-Fi can’t carry raw video → demonstrations must be recorded on the robot’s own computer, exactly as planned


Tablet command rate
~119 messages/sec
the arm wants 100/sec — confirmed feasible


Clock difference laptop ↔︎ robot
~1 second
harmless for recording (one clock does it all); must be synchronized before live deployment





8.1.4 Bottom line
Both pipes work: robot → laptop (all senses readable) and laptop → robot (commands obeyed). The day-1 checklist closed with every box ticked, and the next step is the recording pipeline: capturing human demonstrations on the robot’s own computer in the format the learning software expects.
